---
title: "Exercise: domain shift and adaptation"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- explain why a model trained on one microscope fails on another, and detect a shift without labels,
- apply and judge the remedies: normalisation, re-estimated statistics, augmentation, fine-tuning on a few images,
- recognise the trap of each remedy, in particular a change of the class balance *(math: covariate and label shift)*,
- design an honest evaluation across microscopes and experiments.

The questions under **By hand** and **Explore** are for everyone. The **Math questions** are for students who want the full treatment.

## Background

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Domain | where the images come from: microscope, stain, lab, cell line |
| Domain shift | the images (or the cells) of the new domain differ from the training images |
| Shift score | here: the largest difference of feature means between A and B, in A's standard deviations |
| Standardise | $(f - \text{mean})/\text{SD}$, with the statistics of the images at hand |
| Re-estimated statistics | a network's normalisation layers use the means and variances of the new images |
| Label shift | the share of each class changes, the look of each class does not |

## By hand

**B1.** On microscope A, interphase cells have a mean intensity of about 0.42 and mitotic cells 0.62. Microscope B measures $0.56 \cdot I + 0.096$ (the demo's shift 0.8).
(a) What do the two kinds of cell measure on B?
(b) A rule learnt on A calls a cell mitotic above 0.52. What does it call both kinds of cell on B?

**B2.** Standardisation per microscope. On A the intensities of all cells have mean 0.52 and SD 0.12 (half the cells mitotic).
(a) What are the mean and SD on B (same cells, B's measurement of B1)?
(b) Standardise a mitotic cell on A ($I = 0.62$) and on B. Compare.
(c) Why does any gain $g > 0$ and offset drop out?

**B3.** The class-balance trap. Microscope B is identical to A, but only 20 % of its cells are mitotic.
(a) What is B's mean intensity (classes at 0.42 and 0.62)?
(b) The class SD is 0.08 in both classes, so B's overall SD is about 0.11. Standardise an interphase cell (0.42) and a mitotic cell (0.62) with B's statistics and with A's (mean 0.52, SD 0.12). Which way does B's normalisation push the interphase cells?
(c) What does the shift score report, although the microscope did not change?

**B4.** A normalisation unit in a network stores the mean 2 and SD 1 of its input $z$ (measured on A) and outputs $(z - 2)/1$. On microscope B its input is $z_B = 0.5\,z_A$.
(a) A cell gives $z_A = 3$ on A. What does it give on B, and what does the unit output with the stored statistics?
(b) Re-estimate the statistics on B (mean and SD of $z_B$) and recompute. Compare with A.

**B5.** Choose a remedy (or several) and explain:
(a) A new camera on the same microscope; you have hundreds of unlabelled images.
(b) A new cell line in which mitotic cells are larger than before.
(c) Your model will be used by other labs with microscopes you do not know.
(d) Your training images are fluorescence; the new ones stained tissue sections.

**B6.** You adapted a model to microscope B with 30 labelled images from one B slide, and want to report how well it works on B. Which images do you test on, and what do you report?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) Interphase $0.56 \cdot 0.42 + 0.096 = 0.331$; mitotic $0.56 \cdot 0.62 + 0.096 = 0.443$. (b) Both lie below 0.52: everything is called interphase; every mitotic cell is missed.

**B2.** (a) Mean $0.56 \cdot 0.52 + 0.096 = 0.387$, SD $0.56 \cdot 0.12 = 0.067$. (b) A: $(0.62 - 0.52)/0.12 = 0.83$; B: $(0.443 - 0.387)/0.067 = 0.83$: the same. (c) $(gI + o - (g\mu + o))/(g\sigma) = (I - \mu)/\sigma$: the offset cancels in the difference, the gain in the ratio.

**B3.** (a) $0.8 \cdot 0.42 + 0.2 \cdot 0.62 = 0.46$. (b) With B's statistics: interphase $(0.42 - 0.46)/0.11 = -0.36$, mitotic $(0.62 - 0.46)/0.11 = 1.45$; with A's: $-0.83$ and $0.83$. B's normalisation pushes interphase cells from $-0.83$ to $-0.36$, towards the mitotic side, and a classifier trained on standardised A features calls more of them mitotic. (c) $(0.52 - 0.46)/0.12 = 0.5$ SD: a "shift" caused by biology, not by the microscope (the demo's score: 0.37 for its cells).

**B4.** (a) $z_B = 1.5$; output $(1.5 - 2)/1 = -0.5$, while on A the same cell gives $(3 - 2)/1 = 1$. (b) On B the mean is $0.5 \cdot 2 = 1$ and the SD $0.5$: output $(1.5 - 1)/0.5 = 1$, as on A.

**B5.** (a) Re-estimate the normalisation statistics (or standardise per microscope) on the unlabelled images; check on a few labelled ones. (b) Fine-tune on a few labelled images of the new line: the cells really look different (a change of $p(\mathbf x \mid y)$ that no normalisation undoes). (c) Train with strong augmentation (intensity, blur, noise, pixel size) and evaluate on held-out labs; advise users to check on an annotated subset. (d) Fine-tune all layers on labelled tissue images (a new modality is not an augmentation of the old one).

**B6.** Test on labelled B images from other slides or days than the 30 used for fine-tuning; report the B score with the split level, and the A score separately (to see what was forgotten), not a pooled mean.
:::

### Math questions

**B7.** *(math)* Show that if microscope B measures every feature as $g_kf_k + o_k$ with $g_k > 0$, and the population of cells is the same, then standardising each microscope with its own statistics gives identical features. Which assumption fails in B3?

**B8.** *(math)* Label shift. A calibrated classifier trained on A (50 % mitotic) gives $p_A(\text{mitotic} \mid \mathbf x) = 0.6$. On B, 20 % of the cells are mitotic, and $p(\mathbf x \mid y)$ is unchanged. Using Bayes' rule, show $p_B(y \mid \mathbf x) \propto p_A(y \mid \mathbf x)\,p_B(y)/p_A(y)$ and compute $p_B(\text{mitotic} \mid \mathbf x)$.

**B9.** *(math)* A linear unit $z = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b$ is followed by a normalisation with stored $(\mu, \sigma)$. On B every input is $\mathbf x_B = g\,\mathbf x_A + o\,\mathbf 1$. Show that $z_B = g\,z_A + c$ for a constant $c$, and that re-estimating $(\mu, \sigma)$ on B restores the normalised output exactly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B7.** *(math)* Over the same population, the mean on B is $g_k\mu_k + o_k$ and the SD $g_k\sigma_k$, so $(g_kf_k + o_k - g_k\mu_k - o_k)/(g_k\sigma_k) = (f_k - \mu_k)/\sigma_k$. In B3 the population is not the same (fewer mitotic cells), so B's mean and SD differ from A's for a reason that is not a measurement change, and the standardised features of a given cell differ between A and B.

**B8.** *(math)* $p_B(y \mid \mathbf x) = p(\mathbf x \mid y)p_B(y)/p_B(\mathbf x)$ and $p(\mathbf x \mid y) = p_A(y \mid \mathbf x)p_A(\mathbf x)/p_A(y)$; terms not depending on $y$ go into the proportionality constant. Odds: $\frac{0.6}{0.4} \cdot \frac{0.2/0.5}{0.8/0.5} = 1.5 \cdot 0.25 = 0.375$, so $p_B = 0.375/1.375 = 0.27$.

**B9.** *(math)* $z_B = \mathbf w\cdot(g\mathbf x_A + o\mathbf 1) + b = g(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_A + b) + o\,\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf 1 + b(1 - g) = g z_A + c$. Over the same population, $\mu_B = g\mu_A + c$ and $\sigma_B = \lvert g\rvert\sigma_A$; for $g > 0$, $(z_B - \mu_B)/\sigma_B = (z_A - \mu_A)/\sigma_A$. (After a ReLU the next layer's inputs are no longer an exact affine map of A's, so deeper layers are corrected only approximately: hence layer by layer.)
:::

## Explore: two microscopes {#explore}

Each cell is two numbers: its mean intensity and its size. A classifier (a line in this plane) is trained on 400 cells of microscope A (hollow dots), half of them mitotic. Microscope B (filled dots) measures the intensity on another scale: the **shift** slider goes from no change to a dimmer, raised scale (intensity × 0.45 + 0.12 at shift 1). The **mitotic share in B** slider changes B's population. The remedies: **as is**; **normalise per microscope** (each microscope's features standardised with its own mean and SD; the classifier was trained on standardised A features); **trained with augmentation** (A's intensities randomly scaled and shifted during training); **fine-tuned on 10 B cells** (5 of each class, black dots). The dashed line is the A classifier, the solid line the chosen remedy's, both drawn in B's measurements. Right: accuracy on B against the shift for all remedies, and a shift score that needs no labels.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="domainshift" data-preset="shift"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/domainshift.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **same microscope**, then move the shift slider to 1. Watch the B cloud and the accuracy of "as is". At which shift does it drop below 80 %?

**E2.** Preset **dimmer microscope B** (shift 0.8). Read the shift score and the four accuracies. Which remedy line moves with the B cloud?

**E3.** Preset **normalise per microscope**. Why is its accuracy the same at every shift (the blue curve is flat)?

**E4.** Preset **fewer mitoses in B** (a fifth). What happens to the normalised remedy, also at shift 0? What does the shift score say at shift 0?

**E5.** Preset **fine-tune on 10 B cells**. Compare with the other remedies in the right panel. Where are the 10 cells, and how far does the line move from the dashed A line?

**E6.** Select **trained with augmentation**. How does its line differ from the A line, and what does that cost on microscope A (shift 0, mitotic share 0.5)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** At shift 0 "as is" gets 92.5 % (on these B cells; 96 % on A's own cells). It reaches 80.0 % at shift 0.65 and falls below at 0.7 (77.3 %), to 59.8 % at shift 1. The B cloud slides left (dimmer) and squeezes, and the mitotic cells cross the dashed line.

**E2.** Shift score 1.01 SD. As is 71.0 %, normalised 93.0 %, augmented 85.0 %, fine-tuned 93.0 %. The normalised line (drawn in B's measurements) and the fine-tuned line follow the B cloud; the augmented line is steep (it relies on size) and does not need to move.

**E3.** Standardising B with B's own mean and SD undoes any gain and offset exactly (B2, B7): the standardised B cells are the same numbers at every shift, so the classifier sees the same input: 93.0 %.

**E4.** Normalised: 83.3 % at every shift, also at shift 0 where as is gets 91.8 %: B's lower mean intensity is real (fewer bright cells), and normalisation shifts every B cell towards "mitotic" (B3). The shift score is 0.37 at shift 0: it cannot tell a biological change from a microscope change. As is falls to 85.8 % at shift 0.8, augmented 89.5 %.

**E5.** Fine-tuned: 91.3 % at shift 0.8 with a fifth mitotic, and about 90 to 91 % at every shift: the best remedy here. The 10 labelled cells sit in the B cloud; the line is pulled from the A line to between the B classes (the penalty keeps it close to the A line where the 10 cells allow).

**E6.** The augmented line is nearly horizontal: the classifier relies mostly on size, because intensity was made unreliable in training. On A-like images (shift 0, half mitotic) it reaches about 89 % against 92.5 % for the plain classifier: the price of ignoring an informative feature.
:::

## Code {#code}

Write the algorithms of this unit yourself, in Rust. Setup, and how to run and check your code:
[coding exercises: getting started](../code.qmd). Your code goes in `finetuning/src/domain_shift/exercise.rs`.

`finetuning/src/domain_shift/model.rs` gives the cells of the two microscopes (as in the demo:
`cells_a`, `to_b`) and the classifier (`Linear::fit`, `accuracy`; with a prior and a penalty
it fine-tunes another classifier).

**C1.** `stats(cells)`: the mean and SD (divided by $n$) of each feature. The check is a two-cell example.

**C2.** `standardise(cells, mean, sd)`: $(f - \text{mean})/\text{SD}$ for each feature; the class is kept.

**C3.** `shift_score(a, b)`: $\max_k \lvert\text{mean}_k^B - \text{mean}_k^A\rvert / \text{SD}_k^A$.

**C4.** `augment(cells, copies, seed)`:

```
for every cell, `copies` times:
    gain = 0.4 + 0.8 · uniform();  offset = −0.05 + 0.25 · uniform()
    new cell: intensity = gain · intensity + offset, same size, same class
```

Then `cargo run -p finetuning -- domain-shift`. The program prints A's statistics, the accuracy
of the plain and the augmented classifier on A, their weights, and for shifts 0 to 1 the shift
score and the accuracy on B of the four remedies, with B's mitotic share 0.5 and 0.2.

**C5.** Compare the weights of the plain and the augmented classifier. Which feature does each rely on?

**C6.** Mitotic share 0.5: describe how each remedy behaves as the shift grows.

**C7.** Mitotic share 0.2: which remedy is best at shift 0, and which at shift 1? Why is normalisation worst at shift 0?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (code)"}
The model solution is `finetuning/src/domain_shift/solution.rs` in the download.

The program prints A's mean intensity 0.523 (SD 0.123) and size 0.484 (SD 0.128); the plain classifier gets 95.0 % on A, the augmented one 88.2 %.

**C5.** Plain: (−6.2, 28.8, −17.8) for (constant, intensity, size): it relies more on intensity. Augmented: (7.3, 7.0, −21.6): it relies mostly on size, which augmentation left alone.

**C6.** As is: 94.0, 94.2, 84.0, 72.8, 58.0 % at shifts 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Normalised: 94.8 % at every shift. Augmented: 89.2 % falling slowly to 84.2 %. Fine-tuned on 10 B cells: 92.2 to 94.8 %. The shift score grows from 0.07 to 1.35.

**C7.** Shift 0: as is and fine-tuned (92.5 and 92.8 %); shift 1: fine-tuned (94.0 %), then augmented (89.2 %), as is 84.0 %, normalised 77.2 % at every shift. Normalisation moves B's cells by the difference of the population means, which here is biology (fewer bright mitotic cells), not the microscope; the shift score is 0.49 already at shift 0.
:::

## Where this leads

Domain shift is why the [cell-networks day](../cellnets-compare/lec.qmd) insisted on testing every network on an annotated subset of your own images, and why the [leakage unit](../leakage/lec.qmd) splits by experiment and day. The [self-supervised day](../pretext/lec.qmd) shows another remedy: pretraining on unlabelled images of your own domain, so that the features fit before any label is spent.
